analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal price support and quota program for tobacco farmers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House Agriculture subcommittee and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Rick Santorum's bill would have ended the federal programs that guarantee tobacco growers a minimum price and limit who can sell tobacco, terminating the government-backed loans and winding down the No Net Cost Tobacco Fund on January 1, 1993. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Peanuts and Tobacco subcommittee, where no action was taken. It never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers would no longer back loans and funds supporting the tobacco crop, and federal policy would stop underwriting a product that harms health. Repealing the quota system would also let anyone grow tobacco, ending a licensing system that restricted supply.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the tobacco price support program created under the Agricultural Act of 1949, ending the federal guarantee of a minimum price for tobacco growers.
It repeals the tobacco marketing quota program under the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938, ending the system that limits who may market tobacco.

It directs the Secretary of Agriculture, effective January 1, 1993, to terminate all loan agreements with tobacco producer associations and dispose of the funds in the No Net Cost Tobacco Fund and the related Commodity Credit Corporation account.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco farmers, who would lose guaranteed minimum prices and the value of their marketing quotas, and the rural communities dependent on tobacco growing.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco growers would bear the full loss: the price support program guarantees them a floor price, and marketing quotas are valuable assets; ending both abruptly, with no transition assistance, would hit farming families and tobacco-dependent rural economies hard.

A fair objection supporters of the current program would raise is that the quota and price support system was designed under the 'no net cost' rules to shift program costs onto growers themselves rather than taxpayers, limiting the savings the bill could actually deliver.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending federal support for a harmful crop is sound policy on its face, but this bill offered nothing to ease the transition for growers whose quotas and price guarantees would vanish overnight. The strongest case against the subsidy is also the strongest case for a gradual phase-out paired with transition aid, which this bill did not include.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Peanuts and Tobacco subcommittee, sat there for the rest of the session, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Santorum introduced the bill on March 26, 1992, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day.
On March 31, 1992, it was referred to the subcommittee handling peanuts and tobacco, where no further action was taken.
The bill received no floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers and the tobacco-state members who controlled the House Agriculture Committee's agenda kept the price support and quota system intact. Nothing changed for taxpayers or public health.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco growers and the ag committee

for.name: Rep. Rick Santorum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the tobacco price support and quota programs.

for.name: 6 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill; four Republicans and two Democrats.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Peanuts and Tobacco subcommittee and never brought it up for a committee vote or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's six cosponsors split four Republicans and two Democrats, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan breakdown of actual support or opposition exists in the record.

industries.note: The price support program guarantees growers a minimum price and marketing quotas restrict who can sell tobacco, so repeal would end both protections. Their subsidy exists to keep tobacco prices up, a cost borne by the public whose health the crop damages.
Repealing price supports and quotas would change the cost and supply of leaf tobacco that manufacturers buy, ending a system that had stabilized their raw-material market for decades.
